newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Girl killed as Canberra demolition goes wrong.
newsitem.headline: Girl killed as Canberra demolition goes wrong.

text.p: A 12-year-old Australian girl died and several people were injured in Canberra on Sunday when a hospital demolition went wrong, spewing debris over thousands of spectators who turned out for what had been billed a family event.
Australian Federal Police acting sergeant Darryl Webb told Reuters the girl died during the implosion of the capital's old hospital, on the shore of a lake. Police originally said the victim was 23.
"I was standing next to a boy, he was about 14 or 15...and we saw something skip across the water and then it hit him," a woman witness told local radio.
"We heard him scream out as it hit him," said the woman, who did not give her name.
"Another woman came out of the crowd with blood on her hands and she said that she was behind a girl who was killed by a rock."

Police and government investigations have begun and a counselling service has been set up for the tens of thousands of tourists and locals who had packed the lakeshore and surrounding parks and bridges on a sunny afternoon to watch the event that had been heavily promoted by the regional government.

The main construction union called on local government chief Kate Carnell to stand aside pending a government inquiry into the affair, including the awarding of the contract and the decision to implode rather than tear down the building.
Construction, Forestry, Mining and Energy Union (CFMEU) local branch secretary George Wason criticised the decision.
"Dealing with explosives is always a dangerous affair and there was no need to implode the building," he said.
Carnell, who watched the implosion with her family from the top of a nearby hotel, said she was horrified by the tragedy.
"It appears that something has gone wrong and we need, I need, to find out what that was," she told reporters.
"There was no indication whatsoever that this was even a possibility."
The event had been widely advertised to draw family crowds and a fireworks display was included in the entertainment.
Foreign Minister Alexander Downer's media spokesman, Innes Willox, was standing in the worst hit area with his family.
"There was all this shrapnel raining across the lake in front of us," he said.
Carnell said the company in charge of the demolition had said debris would be confined to within 50 metres (yards) and a 200 metre exclusion zone had been set for added safety.

The dead girl was standing in a park about 400 metres across the lake from the hospital and witnesses said debris had been blasted more than 500 metres from the blast site, about one km (0.6 miles) from parliament house.

The dead girl has not been identified and police would not say where she was from, but Webb said police had confirmed her age after speaking to her shocked parents, after several conflicting reports immediately after the accident.
At least nine people were injured, including a 14-year-old boy with serious chest wounds.
The government inquiry, separate to police investigations, will begin on Monday and be headed by former senior federal official Noel Tanzer, a spokesman for Carnell said.
"We want to get some answers reasonably quickly," he said.
Tanzer is a former head of the Administrative Services Department, which has maintenance responsibilities for federal buildings.
The hospital was closed in 1991 and was being demolished to clear the site for a new national museum.
